items.prompt: What are Git's three areas for a file's state?
choices: Local branch, remote branch, and tag
Working tree, index (staging area), and repository
Stash, reflog, and HEAD
Origin, upstream, and fork
items.explanation: The working tree is the files on disk, the index is the prepared next snapshot, and the repository is committed history.

items.prompt: Which area holds the files exactly as they look on disk right now?
choices: The index
The repository
The stash list
The working tree
items.explanation: The working tree is just the ordinary files in your project folder, including every unsaved-to-Git edit.

items.prompt: What does `git add` do to a changed file?
choices: Copies its current content into the index
Writes it into permanent history
Deletes the edit from the working tree
Sends it to the remote server
items.explanation: git add updates the index with the file's content at that moment, ready for the next commit.

items.prompt: What does `git commit` turn into permanent history?
choices: Whatever is currently on disk
Every file in the project, regardless of staging
The snapshot currently held in the index
Only the files you last edited
items.explanation: A commit records the index, not the working tree, which is why staging matters.

items.prompt: What is `git status` mostly a report of?
choices: Which branches exist on the remote
How many commits you have made today
How the three areas differ from each other
Which files are largest on disk
items.explanation: Status compares working tree to index and index to HEAD and prints the differences.

items.prompt: A brand-new file that was never `git add`ed is in which state?
choices: Untracked
Staged
Committed
Stashed
items.explanation: Git sees the file on disk but has made no promise to track it in history yet.

items.prompt: Which area is the 'prepared snapshot for the next commit'?
choices: The working tree
The repository
The reflog
The index (staging area)
items.explanation: The index is where you assemble exactly what the next commit will contain.

items.prompt: After a successful `git commit`, where is that content permanently recorded?
choices: Only in the working tree
In the repository, as a commit
Only in the index
Only in the stash
items.explanation: Commits are the permanent history; the other areas can be changed or discarded freely.

items.prompt: `a.txt` is committed as v1. You edit it to v2 and run `git add a.txt`, then edit it again to v3. Which versions sit in the working tree, index, and repository?
choices: Working tree v3, index v3, repository v2
Working tree v2, index v2, repository v1
Working tree v3, index v2, repository v1
Working tree v3, index v1, repository v1
items.explanation: git add copied v2 into the index. The later edit only changed the working tree, and nothing has been committed, so HEAD still holds v1.
items.reference:
Three areas, one file
📁 Working tree: the files on disk right now
📋 Index: the snapshot prepared for the next commit
🗃️ Repository: committed history
Why: a single file can hold a different version in each area at the same moment.
items.learnMore:
Three areas, not one 'file'

Most 'where did my change go' confusion comes from picturing one file in one place. Git compares three copies, and git status is the report of how they differ.

Common mistake

Thinking that saving in your editor puts the change into Git. Saving only updates the working tree.
items.reflection: Think of any workflow with a draft, a prepared version, and a final published version, such as a document, a design, or a recipe. Which of those three stages would a careless 'save' leave you in, and what would be lost if only the final version was backed up?

items.prompt: Continuing that situation (working tree v3, index v2, repository v1), you run `git commit`. What does the new commit contain for `a.txt`?
choices: v2, the staged version
v3, the current content on disk
v1, since nothing changed
Both v2 and v3 merged
items.explanation: A commit records the index. The v3 edit was never staged, so it stays as an uncommitted modification.

items.prompt: A teammate says: 'I saved the file in my editor, so my change is safely in Git.' What is actually true?
choices: Saving stages the file automatically, so it is queued for the next commit
Saving commits to the current branch, which records it in history
Saving writes the change into the stash, so it can be recovered later
Saving only updated the working tree; Git has no record of it yet
items.explanation: Editor saves touch the working tree only. Staging and committing are separate, explicit steps.

items.prompt: You create `notes.txt`, run `git add notes.txt`, then delete the file from disk before committing. What does Git still hold?
choices: Nothing at all, because once the file is gone from disk the index drops it
The added content in the index, so it shows as staged and also as deleted in the working tree
The file in the repository as a commit, since add records it permanently
The file in the stash list, where deleted files are kept by default
items.explanation: The index keeps what you added. Status then reports a staged new file plus an unstaged deletion, because disk and index now disagree.

items.prompt: Technically, what is a Git branch?
choices: A full copy of all project files
A movable name that points at a commit
A separate working tree for unfinished edits
A folder inside the repository
items.explanation: A branch is a lightweight pointer to a commit; it does not store files or edits itself.

items.prompt: Are uncommitted edits part of any branch?
choices: Yes, of the branch currently checked out
Yes, of the branch they were first saved on
Yes, of the main branch only
No, they are in no commit at all
items.explanation: Branches point at commits, and an uncommitted edit is not in a commit.

items.prompt: Where do uncommitted edits physically live?
choices: In the working tree (and in the index if staged)
Inside the current branch pointer
In the remote repository
In the reflog
items.explanation: They are ordinary files on disk, optionally staged in the index.

items.prompt: Why can an edit seem to 'follow' you to another branch?
choices: Git copies uncommitted edits between branches automatically on every switch
The edit was committed in the background by the switch before it finished
Checkout left that file alone because it was identical on both commits
Git stashed the edit and then reapplied it to the new branch for you
items.explanation: Checkout only rewrites files that differ between the two commits, so an identical file keeps its working-tree edit.

items.prompt: When does `git checkout <branch>` refuse to switch?
choices: Whenever the working tree has any edits at all
Whenever the target branch is older
When a file with uncommitted changes would be overwritten
Whenever you have staged files
items.explanation: Git refuses only when proceeding could destroy your uncommitted work.

items.prompt: Which pair of actions safely saves unfinished work before switching?
choices: Commit it or stash it
Close the editor
Switch quickly and switch back
Run git status twice
items.explanation: Both commit and stash move the work into the repository, where a branch switch cannot disturb it.

items.prompt: A branch switch finished with no warning. Does that prove your edit was committed?
choices: Yes, Git only switches when everything is committed
Yes, Git commits automatically on a switch
Yes, because the status was clean
No, silent success says nothing about commits
items.explanation: Switching can succeed silently with uncommitted edits still sitting in the working tree.

items.prompt: What habit does this unit recommend before switching with unfinished work?
choices: Rely on Git to keep it with its branch
Decide where the work belongs, then commit or stash it
Delete the file and rewrite it later
Switch first and sort it out afterward
items.explanation: Because uncommitted work has no branch affinity, you have to place it deliberately.

items.prompt: You edit `shared-config.js` on `feature-a` without committing. On `feature-b` the committed file differs and your edit would conflict with it. What does `git checkout feature-b` do?
choices: Switches anyway and silently discards your edit to the diverged file
Switches anyway and commits your edit onto feature-b as a new commit
Switches anyway and moves your edit into the stash for later
Aborts the switch with a 'local changes would be overwritten' error
items.explanation: Git refuses rather than risk destroying the edit. Nothing changes, and you can commit or stash and try again.
items.reference:
Where an edit lives
🏷️ Branch: a name pointing at one commit
✏️ Uncommitted edit: in the working tree, in no commit
🔀 Checkout: moves the label and updates only differing files
Why: an edit not in any commit cannot belong to any branch.
items.learnMore:
Branches label commits, not edits

A branch is just a movable name on a commit. Until you commit, your change is not on the commit graph at all, so it is not attached to the branch you happened to be on.

Common mistake

Saying 'my edit is on feature-a'. Before a commit it is in the shared working tree, and any branch you switch to sees the same files.
items.reflection: Think of a shared whiteboard in a meeting room that several teams use in turn. If you leave notes on it without photographing them, what decides whether they are still there when you return, and what habit protects them?

items.prompt: Why is the sentence 'my edit belongs to feature-a' wrong before you commit?
choices: Edits belong to whichever branch was created first in the repository
The edit is in the shared working tree, not in any commit or branch
Edits belong to main until they have been pushed to the remote server
Edits belong to whichever branch currently has the fewest commits on it
items.explanation: A branch only labels commits. An uncommitted edit is not on the commit graph, so no branch owns it.

items.prompt: Which outcome is riskier for your uncommitted edit: an error refusing the switch, or a silent clean switch?
choices: The silent switch, because nothing signals the edit is still fragile
The refusal, because it blocks your work and leaves the edit stuck in place
They carry identical risk, because both leave the edit uncommitted in the tree
Neither one, because Git always keeps a hidden backup copy of every edit
items.explanation: A refusal forces you to deal with the edit. A silent carry-over leaves it uncommitted and easy to forget or later discard.

items.prompt: A file is identical on both branches, and you staged an edit to it with `git add` (not committed). You switch branches. What happens to the staged edit?
choices: It is committed to the old branch automatically before the switch happens
It is unstaged and lost, because checkout resets the index on every switch
It stays staged and uncommitted, carried along on the new branch
It is moved into the stash and must be popped before you can use it again
items.explanation: Checkout left the file alone, so both the working tree and the index entry remain. Nothing has been committed.

items.prompt: `git status` shows 'changes not staged for commit'. Which two areas are being compared?
choices: Index and repository
Working tree and index
Repository and remote
Stash and working tree
items.explanation: Unstaged changes are edits on disk that differ from what is in the index.

items.prompt: `git status` shows 'changes to be committed'. Which two areas are being compared?
choices: Working tree and index
Working tree and remote
HEAD and the stash
Index and HEAD
items.explanation: Staged changes are differences between the index and the last commit.

items.prompt: You edit a tracked file and do nothing else. Which heading lists it?
choices: Changes not staged for commit
Changes to be committed
Untracked files
Nothing, it is hidden
items.explanation: The edit exists only in the working tree, so it differs from the index.

items.prompt: You edit a file and run `git add` on it, with no later edits. Which heading lists it?
choices: Changes not staged for commit only
Untracked files
Changes to be committed
Both headings equally
items.explanation: After add, the index matches the working tree, and the index differs from HEAD.

items.prompt: How many independent comparisons does `git status` run on tracked files?
choices: One
Three
Two
Four
items.explanation: Working tree vs index, and index vs HEAD.

items.prompt: What does `git add` do to the two lists?
choices: Moves the change from 'not staged' into 'to be committed'
Deletes the change from both lists so that status looks clean again
Copies the change to the remote so teammates can see it immediately
Has no effect on either list until the next commit is made
items.explanation: Add makes the index match the working tree for that file.

items.prompt: Right after `git commit`, what is the index-vs-HEAD difference for the committed file?
choices: The whole file
Half the file
Only the last line
None, the two now match
items.explanation: The commit turned the index snapshot into HEAD.

items.prompt: Why does Git have an index instead of committing straight from disk?
choices: To make commits slower so that every change gets a careful review
So you choose exactly what goes into the next commit
To store a backup copy of every file each time you save in an editor
To encrypt your files before they are written into the repository
items.explanation: The index lets you stage some files or hunks and leave the rest for a later commit.

items.prompt: You edit `a.txt`, run `git add a.txt`, then edit it again. How does `git status` list it?
choices: Under both headings
Only under 'changes to be committed'
Only under 'changes not staged for commit'
Under neither
items.explanation: The index holds the first edit (differs from HEAD) and the working tree holds a second edit (differs from the index).
items.reference:
The two diffs behind git status
🔶 Working tree vs index: 'changes not staged for commit'
🔷 Index vs HEAD: 'changes to be committed'
↔️ One file can appear in both lists at once
Why: status compares neighbouring areas two at a time, never all three at once.
items.learnMore:
Two comparisons, two headings

Because there are three areas, status needs two comparisons to describe a file precisely. Each heading names the pair being compared.

Common mistake

Reading 'to be committed' as 'everything I changed'. It only lists what is already staged.
items.reflection: Imagine a package-shipping process with a packing table, a staged outgoing shelf, and a delivered record. Which comparison would you run to find 'things I changed but did not queue to ship' versus 'things queued but not yet delivered'?

items.prompt: In that same situation you now run `git commit`. What does `git status` report for `a.txt` afterward?
choices: Clean, since the file was committed and nothing differs from HEAD
Untracked, because the commit moved the file out of Git's view
Still modified and not staged, for the second edit
Staged and ready to commit, because the commit staged the edit
items.explanation: The commit recorded only the staged version. The later edit remains a working-tree difference.

items.prompt: A file has two unrelated edits. You stage only one with `git add -p`. How does status list the file?

Under both headings
Only 'not staged'
Untracked
items.explanation: The staged hunk differs from HEAD, and the unstaged hunk differs from the index, so both comparisons find something.

items.prompt: You edit `a.txt` and `git add` it, then manually undo the edit in your editor so the working file equals the original. What does status show?
choices: Clean, because the working file now equals HEAD on disk
Only 'changes to be committed', since the working copy matches HEAD
Only 'changes not staged for commit', since the index is ignored here
Both headings: staged change, plus an unstaged change that reverts it
items.explanation: Index differs from HEAD (staged edit) and working tree differs from index (the revert). Status compares neighbours, not disk against HEAD.

items.prompt: What does checkout compare, per file, to decide what to do?
choices: The file's size and modification time on disk compared across branches
The file's content in the current commit versus the target commit
The author name and date recorded on the last commit touching the file
The number of lines changed since the last time you ran git status
items.explanation: The decision depends on whether the committed content differs between the two commits.

items.prompt: A file is identical in both commits and has an uncommitted edit. What does checkout do?
choices: Overwrites it with the target version
Refuses the switch
Stashes the edit
Leaves the file alone, edit intact
items.explanation: With no committed difference there is nothing to update, so the working tree copy stays.

items.prompt: A file differs between commits and has no local edits. What happens?
choices: It is overwritten with the target commit's version
It is left unchanged, so the old version stays on disk afterward
The switch is refused until you stage the file with git add first
It is staged automatically so you can review it before the switch ends
items.explanation: With nothing local to protect, Git simply updates the file.

items.prompt: A file differs between commits and your local edit conflicts with the target version. What happens?
choices: Your edit is deleted
Your edit is committed
The whole checkout is refused
The conflict is ignored
items.explanation: Git aborts before changing anything and tells you to commit or stash first.

items.prompt: A file differs between commits, but your local edit merges cleanly on top of the target. What may Git do?
choices: Refuse in every case, no matter how small the local change is
Discard the edit silently and switch to the target version anyway
Switch and carry your edit on top of the target's version
Commit the edit for you before switching so that nothing is lost
items.explanation: Git can apply your uncommitted change over the new version when there is no overlap.

items.prompt: You switch branches with an untracked file that the target branch does not contain. What usually happens?
choices: The file stays where it is
It is deleted
It is committed
It is moved into the stash
items.explanation: Git has no committed version to compare, so it leaves untracked files alone.

items.prompt: Does checkout consider which branch you 'meant' an edit for?
choices: Yes, it reads the branch's history to see where the edit started
Yes, it checks the edit's author against the branch's owner first
Yes, it reads your editor's open tabs to guess where you work
No, it only compares the two commits' file contents
items.explanation: Branch intent is not recorded anywhere; only committed content is compared.

items.prompt: A repo has 10,000 files and only 3 differ between two branches. How many does a switch rewrite?
choices: About 3
Half of them
None
items.explanation: Checkout only updates the files that actually differ.

items.prompt: You have uncommitted edits to `a.txt`, `b.txt`, and `c.txt`. Only `b.txt` differs on the target branch, and your edit to it conflicts. What happens when you switch?
choices: Only b.txt blocks the switch, while a.txt and c.txt are moved ahead alone
The entire switch is refused; nothing changes, including `a.txt` and `c.txt`
Git switches and discards your conflicting edit to b.txt, keeping the others
Git switches and commits all three of your edits onto the target branch
items.explanation: Checkout is all-or-nothing. It aborts before touching anything, so your three edits stay exactly as they were.
items.reference:
Checkout's per-file decision
🟰 Same in both commits: file left untouched, edit stays
🔁 Differs, no local edit: overwritten with target version
🧩 Differs, edit merges cleanly: edit carried on top
⛔ Differs, edit conflicts: whole switch refused
Why: checkout asks one question per file: does it differ between these two commits?
items.learnMore:
Checkout is a per-file diff, not a branch move

The cost and the risk of a switch both come from the set of files that differ between the two commits. Everything else is never touched.

Common mistake

Believing a refusal means your whole working tree is at risk. It names only the files whose local changes collide.
items.reflection: Suppose you swap one office's furniture layout for another's, but only move items that differ between the plans. Which items could you leave sitting wherever someone placed them, and which are the ones you must stop and ask about?

items.prompt: You create an untracked `notes.txt`. The target branch has a committed `notes.txt`. What does the switch do?
choices: Silently overwrites your untracked file with the target's committed one
Ignores the target's notes.txt and keeps yours without any message at all
Merges the two files together and stages the result for you to review
Refuses, because it would overwrite your untracked file
items.explanation: Git will not clobber untracked content. It stops with an 'untracked working tree files would be overwritten' error.

items.prompt: A file differs between branches, and your uncommitted edit is in a distant part of it. What may happen on checkout?
choices: It always refuses, because any difference between branches blocks a switch
It always discards the edit, because the target version wins every time
The switch may succeed, with your edit applied on top of the new version
It always commits the edit, because Git must record it before switching
items.explanation: When the two changes do not overlap, Git can combine them. If they overlap, it refuses.

items.prompt: Why does Git not refuse when the file is identical on both branches, even though you have an uncommitted edit?
choices: Nothing would be overwritten, since checkout never rewrites that file
Because identical files are always protected from deletion by Git itself
Because Git commits the edit for you first and then performs the switch
Because the edit is copied into the target branch's history on the way
items.explanation: Refusal is a response to a possible overwrite. With no committed difference, no overwrite is planned.

Why: checkout asks one question per file: does it differ between these two commits?
items.learnMore:
Checkout is a per-file diff, not a branch move

The cost and the risk of a switch both come from the set of files that differ between the two commits. Everything else is never touched.

Common mistake

Believing a refusal means your whole working tree is at risk. It names only the files whose local changes collide.
items.reflection: Suppose you swap one office's furniture layout for another's, but only move items that differ between the plans. Which items could you leave sitting wherever someone placed them, and which are the ones you must stop and ask about?

items.prompt: Which command discards every uncommitted change to tracked files, without asking?
choices: `git status --short`
`git restore .`
`git diff HEAD`
`git log --oneline`
items.explanation: restore . resets the working tree to match the index immediately and silently.

items.prompt: Does a normal `git checkout <branch>` silently destroy a conflicting uncommitted edit?
choices: Yes, always
Yes, but only on main
Yes, if the file is large
No, it refuses instead
items.explanation: Checkout is built to protect conflicting local changes.

items.prompt: Can Git recover an edit that was never committed or stashed?
choices: No
Yes, from the reflog
Yes, from the remote
Yes, with git undo
items.explanation: Git only remembers content that entered the repository.

items.prompt: What does `git reset --hard` do to uncommitted changes in tracked files?
choices: Stashes them
Commits them
Discards them
Stages them
items.explanation: A hard reset makes working tree and index match HEAD, dropping local changes.

items.prompt: Why is the branch switch often blamed for a loss it did not cause?
choices: Checkout always runs last, so it appears to cause whatever just broke
Checkout secretly runs a restore on every file it did not need to change
It is the visible event; the real discard ran earlier and is forgotten
Git writes only branch switches into its logs, so nothing else is visible
items.explanation: People notice the loss after a switch, and misattribute it.

items.prompt: Which command is a safe way to see what is at risk before discarding?
choices: `git status` (or `git diff`)
`git restore .` run on the whole tree
`git reset --hard` run on the branch
`git clean -f` run on the folder
items.explanation: Status and diff only read; they change nothing.

items.prompt: Does `git restore .` ask for confirmation?
choices: Yes, always
Yes, on the main branch
Yes, if files are large
No
items.explanation: That silence is the danger: it acts immediately.

items.prompt: After a destructive discard, where might a copy of your edit still exist?
choices: In the Git reflog, which records every uncommitted change ever made
Outside Git, such as editor history or an OS snapshot
In the index, which keeps old versions of every edited file for you
On the remote server, which receives a copy each time you save
items.explanation: Git cannot help, but other tools may have kept a copy.

items.prompt: In the incident (edit, checkout feature-b, `git restore .`, checkout feature-a), which step actually destroyed the edit?
choices: The first checkout, when the developer switched to feature-b
The final checkout, when the developer returned to feature-a
The `git restore .` on feature-b
The initial edit, which overwrote the committed version in history
items.explanation: Only restore . discarded anything. Both checkouts were uneventful, because the file was identical on both branches.
items.reference:
Who can destroy an uncommitted edit
🔀 git checkout : never overwrites it silently
🧹 git restore . / checkout -- . / reset --hard: discard it, no warning
🚫 Git cannot recover it: never in a commit or stash
Why: only a discard command destroys work; a switch merely changes where you are standing.
items.learnMore:
Find the destructive command, not the visible one

When work vanishes around a branch switch, the switch is rarely the cause. The loss comes from a discard command that ran earlier or later and is easy to forget.

Common mistake

Blaming checkout. Checkout either refuses or leaves the file alone; restore and reset --hard are the commands that throw work away.
items.reflection: Recall a time something you were working on disappeared after you tidied up, such as a deleted draft or an emptied folder. Was the moment you noticed the loss the same as the moment it actually happened?

items.prompt: Two files, `a.txt` and `b.txt`, have uncommitted edits. You run `git restore a.txt`. What happens to `b.txt`?
choices: Its edit is untouched; restore only affected the named path
It is discarded too, because restore always clears the whole tree
It is staged automatically, because restore moves edits into the index
It is committed on the current branch, because restore snapshots the tree
items.explanation: A path argument limits the damage. Only `.` or a broad command reaches everything.

items.prompt: `a.txt` is committed as v1. You edit to v2, `git add`, then edit to v3, then run `git restore .`. What survives?
choices: Nothing survives, because restore . clears the index as well as the disk

v3 survives and v2 is lost, because the newest edit always wins
v2 survives in the index; v3 is lost
items.explanation: restore . resets the working tree from the index. The staged v2 is exactly what it restores, but the unstaged v3 is gone.

items.prompt: You create a brand-new untracked file and run `git restore .`. What happens to it?
choices: It is deleted from disk, because restore . removes unknown files
Nothing, because it has no tracked version to restore
It is committed to the branch, because restore . records every file
It is staged, because restore . adds new files to the index first
items.explanation: restore works on tracked content. Deleting untracked files needs a different command, such as git clean.

items.prompt: Which habit would have prevented losing the edit in the incident?
choices: Switching faster
Committing or stashing before switching
Closing the terminal
Using a different editor
items.explanation: Work inside a commit or stash is out of reach of a cleanup in the working tree.

items.prompt: What does `git stash` do?
choices: Deletes the changes permanently so the working tree starts out clean
Pushes the changes to the remote so that teammates can review them
Commits the changes to main with an automatic message on your behalf
Saves uncommitted changes in a stash entry and cleans the working tree
items.explanation: The stash is a dedicated place in the repository for shelved work.

items.prompt: How do you reapply stashed work?
choices: `git stash pop`
`git stash drop`
`git restore .`
`git reset --hard`
items.explanation: pop reapplies the latest stash entry and removes it from the list.

items.prompt: Is stashed work sitting in the working tree?
choices: Yes, hidden
Yes, in the index
No, it lives in the stash list
Yes, on the remote
items.explanation: That is why a working-tree discard cannot touch it.

items.prompt: Is a throwaway 'wip' commit an acceptable way to protect work?
choices: No, commits must always be perfect
No, only stashes are allowed
Yes, it can be amended or squashed later
Yes, but only on main
items.explanation: A temporary commit is cheap and gets the work into the repository.

items.prompt: For scratch changes you really want to discard, what is the safest approach?
choices: Check status, then restore the exact file path
Run `git restore .` and then check what happened afterward
Run `git reset --hard` to be certain everything is the same
Switch branches and hope that the scratch edits are left behind
items.explanation: Naming the path limits the discard to what you intend.

items.prompt: You are unsure what is uncommitted. What should you do before any discard command?
choices: Run `git reset --hard`
Delete the project folder
Switch branches
Run `git status` and read it
items.explanation: Looking first costs nothing and reveals what is at risk.

items.prompt: Which kind of work survives a `git restore .` run on another branch?
choices: Work in the working tree
Work already in a commit or stash
Work you saved in your editor
Work you remember making
items.explanation: Only the repository's own storage is outside the working tree's reach.

items.prompt: Right after the edit on `feature-a` you run `git stash`, switch to `feature-b`, run `git restore .`, and switch back. What happened to the edit?
choices: It was discarded by the restore . on feature-b, like any uncommitted edit
It was committed to feature-b automatically when the stash was popped
It was merged into main when the developer switched back to feature-a
It survived in the stash and can be restored with `git stash pop`
items.explanation: The restore only affects the working tree. The stash entry lives in the repository.
items.reference:
Move work somewhere safe first
💾 Belongs to this branch: add and commit
📦 Useful but not ready: git stash
🗑️ Truly scratch: restore with an exact path
❓ Unsure: run git status, discard nothing
Why: only content inside the repository survives a broad discard on another branch.
items.learnMore:
The fix is a habit, not a command

The working tree has no per-branch memory, so safety comes from placing work in the repository (a commit or a stash) before you do anything that could touch it.

Common mistake

Believing stash saves everything. By default it skips untracked files unless you add the -u flag.
items.reflection: Where in your daily work do you rely on 'I'll remember not to touch that' instead of putting the thing somewhere that cannot be disturbed? What would the equivalent of a stash be there?

items.prompt: Your edit is finished work for the current branch. Which action best protects it?
choices: Switch branches and rely on the edit staying put in the working tree
`git add` and `git commit` on the current branch
Run `git restore .` so the edit is reset to a known committed state
Run `git stash` and then forget about it until the next time you remember
items.explanation: It belongs in history on this branch, so a commit both protects and places it correctly.
